paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is an autosomal dominant disorder with clinical features that overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Reported features include aortic aneurysm and dissection, mitral valve disease, craniofacial findings such as hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, and retrognathia, and skeletal findings such as tall stature, arachnodactyly, and joint hypermobility. Severity varies widely within and between families. Some carriers have no cardiovascular involvement, and one reported patient had growth retardation, low muscle mass, and distal arthrogryposis (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Bertoli-Avella et al., 2015; Kuechler et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European-American girl born to nonconsanguineous, healthy parents who had 2 older healthy children. From birth she had distal arthrogryposis with contractures of the fingers and toes, hypotonia, failure to thrive, growth retardation, and delayed gross motor development. Her motor examination showed decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength of 1/5, low tone, and diminished reflexes throughout, and subcutaneous fat was markedly reduced. She had a positive Gower sign and a waddling gait, and muscle biopsy showed type 1 fiber predominance. Other features were bifid uvula, retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, blue sclerae, a metopic ridge, a tubular nose, a midline facial nevus flammeus, long narrow hands and feet with arachnodactyly, hyperextensible large joints, mild pectus excavatum, pes planus, and coxa valga. She had no cardiac defect or aortic dilatation, no intellectual disability, and no scoliosis.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with clinical features overlapping with Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes. Seven family members, aged between 40 and 68 years, had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four members had mitral valve abnormalities, ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation that required surgery. Two had iliac and subclavian artery aneurysms, and 1 bruised easily. Craniofacial abnormalities were rather subtle and included a long face, a high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Some family members had pectus deformity, scoliosis, velvety skin, varices, hiatal hernia, HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, or celiac disease. Aortic tissue from 2 members showed elastic fiber fragmentation and medial degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) also described 10 further families (families 2 to 11). Some members had type A or type B aortic dissection, and 1 died from dissection of a cerebral aneurysm. Other cardiovascular findings included mitral valve disease, patent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. Typical Loeys-Dietz features were common, including hypertelorism, bifid uvula and cleft palate, cervical spine instability, and clubfoot. Other recurrent features were dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, tall stature, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, and inguinal hernia. One patient had short stature, and 2 had early-onset osteoarthritis. The medical records showed no evidence of ectopia lentis, and there was no arterial tortuosity. Aortic wall tissue showed elastic fiber fragmentation with deposition of collagen and proteoglycans.

Vascular involvement ranged from none at age 64 years to type A or B dissection and death from dissection of a cerebral aneurysm.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) studied a girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, hypertelorism, low muscle mass, and growth retardation. Exome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous c.1226G-A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution, and Sanger sequencing confirmed that it was de novo. The mutation was absent from her parents and her 2 unaffected sibs. The patient also carried a de novo nonsense mutation (Q70X) in the CDH2 gene, which the authors considered unlikely to drive the phenotype. Cys409 is the penultimate cysteine of the cysteine knot, a residue that is conserved in all TGF-beta family ligands and is essential for ligand activity. In cultured cells, the C409Y mutant ligand did not activate a TGF-beta reporter. When the mutant was coexpressed with wildtype TGFB3 in Xenopus embryos, pSMAD2 and pERK1/2 signaling fell to about 40% and 60% of wildtype, respectively, consistent with a dominant-negative effect. paragraphs.text: In a father and his 2 children with tall stature, arachnodactyly, hyperextensible joints, hypertelorism, and bifid uvula, but no cardiac, aortic, or eye involvement, Kuechler et al. (2015) used exome sequencing to identify a heterozygous c.898C-G transversion in the TGFB3 gene, predicting an arg300-to-gly (R300G) substitution. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and its segregation with the phenotype. The authors suggested that mutations at codon arg300 presumably increase TGF-beta signaling.
